name: Shanta
definition: Shanta is a composite portrait of a woman in her late thirties working in one of Nanjangud's silk-reeling units, navigating the demands of factory work, household care and farming in a taluk known for its sugarcane, paddy and temple festivals. She represents the generation of women in Mysuru's rural-industrial belt who balance wage labour with unpaid family responsibilities, education aspirations for their children and the pressures of Cauvery-dependent irrigation.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shanta works six-day weeks at a privately owned silk-reeling unit on the edge of Nanjangud town, where she stands at a reeling basin from eight in the morning until five in the evening, drawing raw silk thread from boiled cocoons. Her hands are perpetually damp, her fingers calloused from the hot water and the repetitive motion of guiding the fine filament onto wooden reels. She earns around nine thousand rupees a month, paid fortnightly, with no written contract and unpaid leave deducted without question. The unit employs forty women, most from nearby villages, and the supervisor docks pay if the thread breaks too often or the weight falls short. Cocoon prices fluctuate with the season and the Chinese import market, so when the unit's orders slow she is sent home for a week at a stretch with no income. Her husband Nanjappa farms their three acres of mulberry and paddy, selling cocoons to the Ramanagara market or local traders and relying on canal water from the KRS system; in a deficient monsoon the second paddy crop fails and they borrow from the cooperative. Shanta rises at five to cook, feeds the household, walks twenty minutes to catch the seven o'clock KSRTC bus under the Shakti scheme, and returns by half past six to cook again, wash and help her daughter with homework under a single bulb.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shanta lives in a two-room house with a tile roof and a small veranda in a hamlet three kilometres from Nanjangud town, sharing the compound with Nanjappa's widowed mother and his unmarried younger brother who drives an auto-rickshaw in town. Shanta was married at nineteen, shortly after completing second PU in Nanjangud; her parents, small farmers in a neighbouring village, arranged the match through a Vokkaliga network and paid a modest dowry of jewellery and cash. She has two children: a daughter Preethi, fourteen, studying in ninth standard at the government high school in the village, and a son Suraj, eleven, in sixth standard at the same school. Preethi is bright and wants to study science in PU, but Shanta worries about the cost of private college in Mysuru and whether the girl will be safe commuting daily. Suraj is less interested in books and helps his father in the field after school, learning to judge cocoon quality and operate the pump. Shanta's mother-in-law manages the kitchen garden and the two goats, grumbles about Shanta's long hours away from home, and expects her daughter-in-law to lead all the cooking for festivals and family functions. Nanjappa is supportive but leaves the children's schooling entirely to Shanta, saying he finished only seventh standard and cannot help with English or science. The household's income—Shanta's wages, Nanjappa's crop sales, his brother's auto earnings and occasional MGNREGA days—varies sharply with the monsoon and the silk market, and they have an outstanding loan of sixty thousand rupees from a microfinance SHG for a borewell that yielded brackish water.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shanta herself studied in the Kannada-medium government school in her natal village and completed second PU at a government college in Nanjangud, stopping because her parents could not afford the fees and hostel costs for a degree and because marriage was the expected next step. She can read Kannada newspapers and do household accounts, and she wishes she had continued to become a teacher. Her daughter Preethi attends the government high school a kilometre from home, travelling by bicycle now that the Shakti scheme has freed up money for the purchase; before that she walked with classmates, and in the monsoon the mud path made her late or absent. Preethi studies well, scoring above seventy percent in the eighth-standard exams, and she wants to take science in PU and become a lab technician or nurse. Shanta dreams of sending her to a private PU college in Mysuru or Nanjangud where English instruction and better teachers might open a government job, but the fees are fifteen thousand a year and the bus fare, even under Shakti, means two hours of travel each day; Shanta worries about her safety and whether the girl will be teased or fall behind in English. Suraj is in sixth standard, a restless boy who prefers the field to the classroom and whose marks hover around fifty percent. The school has two toilets but no science lab, and the English teacher has been on long leave for six months. Shanta attends parent meetings when she can get leave from the unit, and she has joined the School Development and Monitoring Committee, pushing for a drinking-water filter and repair of the cracked classroom roof.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shanta suffers from chronic lower-back pain and tingling in her wrists, which she attributes to standing all day at the reeling basin and the repetitive strain of guiding thread. The unit has no seating, no fans in summer and poor ventilation, and the air smells of boiled cocoons. She takes paracetamol from the village Janaushadhi shop when the pain is sharp, but she has never consulted a doctor because the nearest PHC is four kilometres away, open only in the mornings, and the doctor is often absent. For her mother-in-law's diabetes and her son's childhood vaccinations the family travels to the Nanjangud community health centre or, in emergencies, to Mysuru's KR Hospital, twenty-five kilometres away. Shanta had both her children delivered at the PHC with the help of an ASHA worker, and she received the Janani Suraksha cash benefit each time, but her second delivery was complicated and she was referred to Mysuru by ambulance in the night. She worries about her daughter reaching puberty and the need for pads, nutrition and information; the school has no health counsellor and the anganwadi in the hamlet closed years ago for lack of a worker. Nanjappa drinks occasionally, more heavily when the crop fails or cocoon prices fall, and twice he has come home drunk and angry, though he has never struck her. Shanta's own mother died young of an undiagnosed illness, and she fears the same, knowing that women in her family and community rarely seek care until it is too late. The microfinance SHG she belongs to organised a health camp last year where she learned her haemoglobin was low, but the iron tablets the ASHA gave her ran out and she has not asked for more.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shanta's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant cultivating caste in the Nanjangud taluk and across Mysuru district, and they observe its marriage and festival customs, drawing social and economic support from a dense network of kin and caste fellows. Her husband's family has farmed the same land for three generations, and her father-in-law, before he died, was a member of the village Vokkaliga sangha that mediated disputes and organised the annual temple fair. Shanta's own father is a small farmer from a Vokkaliga hamlet five kilometres away, and her brother works in a sugar mill in Mandya; visits between the two families happen on festival days and for life-cycle ceremonies. The family worships at the Srikanteshwara Temple in Nanjangud during the annual car festival in March, joining thousands of pilgrims for the event, and they make an annual offering of jaggery and coconut at the small Kalamma temple in their hamlet. Shanta fasts on Varalakshmi Vratam and Gowri festival days, decorating the threshold with rangoli and praying for the wellbeing of her children and husband. Her mother-in-law is more devout and insists on stricter ritual observance, criticising Shanta for missing the evening lamp and for working outside the home. Shanta's SHG, run under NABARD's linkage programme, has ten women from the village, mostly Vokkaliga but including two SC women; they meet fortnightly, save small sums and borrow for school fees, medical bills and farm inputs. The group is her main space for conversation outside the household, though caste and economic differences are rarely discussed openly. She has heard of the Adichunchanagiri Mutt's scholarship schemes for Vokkaliga students but does not know how to apply, and the family has never visited the mutt.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Shanta's family holds a yellow ration card and collects ten kilograms of rice a month under Anna Bhagya from the fair-price shop in the village, though the shop is often closed and the rice is sometimes mixed with stones. Her husband has a Bhoomi land record and a Raitha Sangha membership card, but he does not attend the sangha meetings regularly and dismissed the last Cauvery-release agitation as a distraction. Shanta has an Aadhaar card, a voter ID and a bank account that her SHG insists on, and her wages are paid in cash fortnightly without a payslip; she has never been offered ESIC or any labour welfare. She travels free on KSRTC buses under the Shakti scheme, which has saved her nearly two thousand rupees a month and made it possible to work in town; before Shakti she often walked to save the fare. She has heard of the Gruha Jyothi electricity subsidy and assumes her household benefits, though she does not see the bills; water comes from a borewell they dug with an SHG loan, and the village tap connections are dry most of the year. She attended a gram sabha once when the SDMC election was held, but the men did most of the talking and she left early to cook. The anganwadi in the hamlet has been shut for three years and the panchayat has done nothing; the ASHA worker visits occasionally but has no medicines or supplies. Shanta knows nothing of the Aspirational District programme or MGNREGA entitlements beyond the few days her husband sometimes works on road repair. She distrusts officials and believes that schemes are for people with connections, not families like hers.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shanta worries most about her daughter's future: will she be allowed to study beyond tenth standard, will the family afford PU college, will she be safe travelling to Mysuru, and will she end up married at eighteen and working in a silk unit like her mother? She is proud that Preethi studies well and dreams of a government job for her, something with a salary, respect and security, but she knows that without English-medium schooling and without money for coaching the dream is fragile. She resents the silk unit's casual cruelty—the docked pay, the absence of leave, the supervisor's gendered scolding—but she needs the income and believes there is no alternative. She blames no one in particular for the state of the village school or the closed anganwadi, only a vague sense that the government is for towns and cities, not for people like her. She is grateful for Shakti and believes the Congress government has done something real for women, though she wishes there were doctors at the PHC and that the electricity were more reliable. She does not follow state politics closely and has only a dim sense of the Cauvery dispute, knowing that canal water is life but not understanding the legal or inter-state details. She takes pride in the Srikanteshwara Temple festival and in Mysuru's Dasara, which she has attended twice, seeing them as markers of a dignified local tradition. She believes that girls should be educated as far as money and safety allow, that sons should respect their mothers, and that hard work will be rewarded if luck is kind, though her own experience leaves her uncertain.
